drills.title: vs Himanshu_Nagar04 (882) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black's whole plan was to harass your rook on b7 with ...Bg4, gaining time while you had nothing productive to do with your king on c6. That's exactly what happened: after Kc6 Bg4, your rook gets tied down, and by Kd6 Kf8 Re7 you're babysitting the rook instead of escorting your pawns home. Kb4 was the move — it heads toward the queenside while staying flexible against ...Bh3, and after Kb4 Bh3 Kc5 Kd8 Kd6 Kc8 your king marches the win forward instead of getting stuck defending. In a winning endgame, walk your king toward the action, not away from your rook's support.

drills.coachNote: Black wanted to gain time with ...Bh3 and ...Bg4, harassing your rook on b6 while marching his own king to c5 to contest the win. Kb5 let that happen for free — after Bh3 Kc5 Bg4 you still had to retreat with Rb2 anyway, except now Black's king had already arrived exactly where he wanted it. Rb2 immediately does the same retreat before Black gains anything, so after Rb2 Bh3 Ka3 Bg4 Rh2 Kc6 it's your king making progress, not his. When a retreat is coming regardless, play it first and deny the free tempo.

drills.coachNote: White's queen and bishop share the h6-f8 diagonal, and Qxf8 there is mate — your rook on f8 can't be saved by anything except taking the queen out of the attack. Rh7 moved the wrong rook and never touched that diagonal, so White simply played Qxf8#, and the game was over on the spot. Qh7 was the move: offering the trade forces Qxh7+ Kxh7, wiping the attacking queen off the board, and after Bf4 Re8 Rxe8 you're just consolidating a position that had been completely fine. When mate is one move away on a diagonal, your candidates are moves that block, defend, or trade the attacker — check that first.

drills.coachNote: White had e4 covered twice — the knight on c3 and the bishop on d3 both watch that square, so anything landing there without support just gets eaten. Your knight jump to e4 did exactly that: White played Nxe4, and after Qd8 N4g3 c5 you were down a piece for nothing in an otherwise level game. Nbd7 was the calm move, finishing development and keeping the center solid, and after Rd1 Re8 Ne4 Qxd2 Nxd2 you'd have reached a comfortable, balanced middlegame instead. Before jumping a piece into the center, count attackers and defenders on that square — two attackers and zero defenders is a piece down, not an outpost.

The mate was g5#: the pawn checks the king on f4 while h6 defends g5, and with zero flight squares anywhere, that's game over.
